What happens when faces are quickly flashed in one's peripheral vision? Summarize the role of peripheral vision in the flashed face distortion effect in 200 words or fewer.

name: read
content:
1	In our lifetimes, we encounter hundreds of thousands of faces. Each person's unique exposure to
     2	faces largely determines their "face space"—a model of how we encode, perceive, and remember the
     3	faces that we see.
     4	 Cross-cultural differences, such as the other-race effect, demonstrate that we are generally more
     5	accurate at recognizing faces of ethnicities we are more familiar with. But even within cultures,
     6	people differ greatly in which faces will elicit a sense of trustworthiness, approachability, or
     7	attractiveness.
     8	 Another factor has an even greater effect on how we perceive a face—where the face is positioned
     9	relative to our central or peripheral vision. Something very strange happens when a sequence of
    10	faces is quickly presented in our peripheral vision. This was first demonstrated in 2011 in a
    11	powerful illusion discovered by Jason Tangen, Sean Murphy, and Matthew Thompson, called the "flashed
    12	face distortion effect"
    13	
    14	
    15	 After a few seconds of staring at the central fixation cross, the faces peripherally presented
    16	faces start to appear deformed, cartoonish, and even grotesque. However, upon closer inspection, one
    17	can tell the faces are perfectly normal and have not been altered.
    18	 Several studies have attempted to explain the mechanisms underlying this phenomenon. Is it the fact
    19	that the faces are aligned at the eyes? Is it because they are presented quickly (4-5 faces per
    20	second)? Is it dependent on which faces follow each other or how centrally or peripherally they are
    21	shown?
    22	
    23	
    24	 The Role of Peripheral Vision
    25	 A study by Bowden et al. (2019) explored the role of peripheral vision. We know that everything in
    26	peripheral vision looks blurry compared to central vision. This is because peripheral stimuli are
    27	processed by retinal rod cells that have poor spatial acuity. So it could be that the intrinsic blur
    28	of peripheral vision makes the faces appear distorted.
    29	 However, Bowden et al. compared peripherally presented faces to centrally presented faces
    30	manipulated by blur. Although they found some evidence of face distortion in central vision using
    31	blurred faces, the effect was much larger when using un-blurred peripheral faces.
    32	 Another study by Balas and Pearson (2019) tested additional factors that may influence the
    33	illusion. They again found that peripheral presentation makes a big difference, as does the
    34	presentation speed.
    35	 Notably, the orientation of the faces presented did not seem to matter. In other words, upside-down
    36	faces produced a similar distortion effect as upright faces. This is surprising because, in most
    37	aspects of face perception, upside-down faces produce weak effects due to their general
    38	unfamiliarity (a prime example of this is the Thatcher Effect).
    39	 Do We All Perceive the Same Distortions When Looking at Peripherally Flashed Faces?
    40	 Earlier research by Afraz and Cavanagh (2009) found that peripheral distortion effects are quite
    41	idiosyncratic. Their study presented participants with faces and other stimuli in different
    42	positions of their peripheral vision. Participants were asked to make various judgments, such as the
    43	gender and age of faces or the aspect ratio of shapes.
    44	 They found that the very same stimulus can appear differently depending on where it is placed
    45	within the observer's peripheral vision. For example, a neutral face might appear male in the upper
    46	right corner, but in the lower right corner, the same face might appear female. These differences
    47	are stable over time for a particular observer but vary substantially between observers.
    48	 Therefore, the particularities of the visual distortions we experience in peripheral vision may be
    49	responsible for the particular ways flashed faces appear distorted. Further research is needed to
    50	identify the neural mechanisms behind these effects, whether they occur when we observe non-human
    51	faces, and whether they serve any adaptive purpose.

When a sequence of faces is quickly flashed (4–5 per second) in peripheral vision, they begin to look deformed, cartoonish, and even grotesque, though they are actually normal. Peripheral vision plays a central role in this "flashed face distortion effect."

Bowden et al. (2019) tested whether the effect stems from the intrinsic blur of peripheral vision, which arises because peripheral stimuli are processed by retinal rod cells with poor spatial acuity. They compared blurred central faces with unblurred peripheral faces and found that while blur produced some distortion in central vision, the effect was much larger with unblurred peripheral faces—so blur alone cannot explain the illusion.

Balas and Pearson (2019) confirmed that peripheral presentation makes a big difference, as does presentation speed. Notably, face orientation did not matter: upside-down faces produced similar distortions as upright ones.

Afraz and Cavanagh (2009) showed that peripheral distortion effects are idiosyncratic—the same face can appear male in one corner of peripheral vision and female in another. These differences are stable within an observer but vary between observers. Thus, the particularities of each person's peripheral visual distortions may be responsible for the specific ways flashed faces appear distorted.

Balas and Pearson (2019) confirmed that peripheral presentation makes a big difference, as does presentation speed. Notably, face orientation did not matter: upside-down faces produced similar distortions as upright ones.

Afraz and Cavanagh (2009) showed that peripheral distortion effects are idiosyncratic—the same face can appear male in one corner of peripheral vision and female in another.
